channel.title: LIMap Articles
channel.description: What liminal spaces are, where the word comes from, how they differ from the Backrooms and dreamcore, and real examples in Japan. Articles by LIMap.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in Tokyo: 8 Real Places, From Deep Station Passages to a Rooftop Ferris Wheel
item.description: Eight real places in Tokyo where you can feel a liminal atmosphere, chosen from spots on LIMap: the Keiyo Line passage built in space meant for the Narita Shinkansen, a Marunouchi walkway converted from a car park, the Asakusa underground street from 1955, and a rooftop Ferris wheel. Plus practical notes for visiting.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in Kanagawa, Chiba and Saitama: 8 Real Places, From an Underground Temple to Showa-Era Stations
item.description: Eight real places in Kanagawa, Chiba and Saitama where you can feel a liminal atmosphere, chosen from spots on LIMap: Kokudo Station from 1930, Nebukawa Station above the sea, the former Narita Airport Station, the "underground temple" flood channel, and ruins to view from outside. Plus practical notes.

item.title: Visiting the "Underground Temple": A Guide to Tours of the Metropolitan Area Outer Underground Discharge Channel
item.description: A practical guide to touring the Metropolitan Area Outer Underground Discharge Channel in Kasukabe, Saitama, known as the "underground temple": how to book, the seven courses, age and clothing rules, what happens on rainy days, and how to get there, based on the official information.

item.title: Liminal Amusement Parks: 9 Real Places, From Department-Store Rooftops to Closed Parks
item.description: The mix of nostalgia and unease in an empty amusement park. Rooftop amusement parks on department stores, a Ferris wheel on a building, a 10-yen game corner, closed parks, and a park abroad that came back from ruin: nine places on LIMap.

item.title: Liminal Places Under Water: 7 Real Places, From Villages Beneath Dams to a Bridge That Comes and Goes
item.description: A village and a village office at the bottom of dam lakes, a railway bridge that appears and disappears with the water level, a forest flooded only in spring, and a town in Argentina swallowed by a lake. Seven submerged places, with when to see them and how to visit respectfully.

item.title: Liminal Underground Malls and Passages: 11 Real Places, From Showa-Era Arcades to a Tunnel Under the Sea
item.description: Windowless and without clues to the time, underground malls are classic liminal spaces. From the 1955 Asakusa Underground Shopping Street and the curving Sun Road in Nagoya to cobbled Tenjin, Sapporo's Chi-Ka-Ho and the Kanmon tunnel under the sea: 11 places, with quiet times and tips.

item.title: Liminal Stations: 9 Real Places, From 462 Steps Underground at Doai to Stations With No Road
item.description: Doai, where you descend 486 steps to the platform; Tsutsuishi, inside a tunnel; Koboro and Tsubojiri, with no road; Tamoto on a cliff; and Kowada, where village life has vanished. Nine liminal stations in Japan, with practical notes on return trains and bears.

item.title: What Is Weirdcore? Meaning, Features, and How It Differs From Dreamcore and Liminal Spaces
item.description: Weirdcore is an internet aesthetic that uses deliberately amateurish, low-quality images to evoke confusion, unease and nostalgia for times you never lived. Its motifs, when it emerged, how it differs from dreamcore and liminal spaces, and a word of caution.

item.title: 7 Games Where You Can Walk Through Liminal Spaces: The Exit 8, Pools, Escape the Backrooms and More
item.description: Seven games that let you walk through liminal spaces and the Backrooms: The Exit 8, Platform 8, Pools, Escape the Backrooms, Dreamcore, Anemoiapolis and The Backrooms 1998. Developers, release dates, platforms, how scary they are, language support, and real places that feel like them.

item.title: What Is the Game Pools? Is It Scary? Where Can You Play It? The Poolrooms Game, and Real Places That Feel Like Pools
item.description: A guide to Pools (POOLS), the game about wandering endless tiled swimming pools: who made it, the Poolrooms that inspired it, platforms and language support, what kind of fear it offers, and real pool facilities that feel like it.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in Shizuoka and Tokai: 8 Real Places, From Escalators of Light to a Showa-Era Station
item.description: Eight real places in Shizuoka, Gifu and Mie where you can feel the atmosphere of a liminal space, chosen from spots registered on LIMap: the free observation lobby of the Shizuoka Prefectural Office, the escalators of the MOA Museum of Art, the Site of Reversible Destiny, Yanagase arcade, Ceramic Park MINO, a harbor observation room in Yokkaichi, Ujiyamada Station and Tokuyama Dam. With tips for visiting.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in North Kanto: 9 Real Places, From an Underground Quarry to the Top Floors of Prefectural Offices
item.description: Nine real places in Ibaraki, Tochigi and Gunma where you can feel the atmosphere of a liminal space, chosen from spots registered on LIMap: Tsukuba Center Square, the Art Tower Mito, the underground quarry of the Oya History Museum, prefectural office observation decks open late, the Gunma Music Center, and the Megane Bridge and disused railway. With tips for visiting.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in Okinawa: 7 Real Places, From a Beach Under an Elevated Road to Japan's Southernmost Arcade
item.description: Seven real places in Okinawa where you can feel the atmosphere of a liminal space, chosen from spots registered on LIMap: shopping arcades in Naha and Koza, Naminoue Beach with an elevated road in front, a causeway across the sea, Nago City Hall by Team Zoo, an exhibition hall from the 1975 Ocean Expo and Japan's southernmost arcade on Ishigaki Island. With tips for visiting.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in Hokuriku and Koshinetsu: 8 Real Places, From a Meiji-Era Railway Tunnel to a Library of Round Windows
item.description: Eight real places in the Hokuriku and Koshinetsu regions of Japan where you can feel the atmosphere of a liminal space, chosen from spots registered on LIMap: a Meiji-era railway tunnel turned walking path, the Kiyotsu Gorge Tunnel, a library and art museum in Kanazawa, Toyama's Kansui Park, a free observation deck in Niigata, the Chino Cultural Complex and a mining ruin on Sado Island. With tips for visiting.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in Chugoku and Shikoku: 9 Real Places, From Kenzo Tange's Prefectural Office to Abandoned Railway Lines
item.description: Nine real places in the Chugoku and Shikoku regions of Japan where you can feel the atmosphere of a liminal space, chosen from spots registered on LIMap: Takamatsu's long arcade and the Kagawa Prefectural Office, a waste plant walkway and an underground mall in Hiroshima, the former Taisha Station, Wakasa Station, the former Kurayoshi Line, the Bizan Ropeway and Besshi's Tonaru. With tips for visiting.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in Tohoku: 8 Real Places, From a Ferry That Will Never Sail to a White Art Museum
item.description: Eight real places in the Tohoku region of Japan where you can feel the atmosphere of a liminal space, chosen from spots registered on LIMap: a museum ferry and an art museum in Aomori, Sendai Mediatheque, a free observation deck in Akita, a former bank in Morioka, a former prefectural office in Yamagata, Aizu's Sazaedo and a department store dining hall in Hanamaki. With tips for visiting.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in Kyushu: 9 Real Places, From an Undersea Pedestrian Tunnel to a Showa-Era Steel Tower
item.description: Nine real places in Kyushu where you can feel the atmosphere of a liminal space, chosen from spots registered on LIMap: the Kanmon pedestrian tunnel, Tenjin Underground Mall, Hakata Port Tower, the Wakato ferry, Nagasaki's inclined elevator and Gunkanjima. With tips for visiting.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in Hokkaido: 9 Real Places, From Sapporo's Underground Walkways to a Bridge That Sinks Into a Lake
item.description: Nine real places in Hokkaido where you can feel the atmosphere of a liminal space, chosen from spots registered on LIMap: Sapporo's underground walkway and mall, an Isamu Noguchi park, a disused railway in Otaru, a museum ferry in Hakodate and a bridge that sinks into a lake. With tips for visiting.

item.title: Liminal Spaces in Nagoya: 8 Real Places, From Underground Malls to Showa-Era Public Buildings
item.description: Eight real places in Nagoya where you can feel the atmosphere of a liminal space, chosen from spots registered on LIMap: underground malls from 1957, a city hall with a 100-meter corridor, a red-brick former courthouse and a glass roof covered in water. With tips for visiting.

item.title: Liminal Space Photo Spots in Kansai: Real Places in Osaka, Kobe, Nara and Shiga
item.description: Real liminal spaces you can visit in the Kansai region of Japan, chosen from spots registered on LIMap: an artificial island in Kobe, the world's first capsule hotel, the remains of a railway bridge and an ore-dressing plant, plus tips for visiting.

item.title: Is the Backrooms Movie Scary? A Spoiler-Free Guide to What Kind of Fear It Uses
item.description: How frightening is Backrooms, really? With no plot spoilers at all: why its fear is spatial rather than jump-scare based, why reviews are split, and how to tell whether it is for you if horror is not your thing.

item.title: Where to Go in Tokyo After Watching the Backrooms Movie
item.description: If the film changed how your commute looks, here are real places in Tokyo with a similar atmosphere, taken from spots actually recorded on LIMap: underground passages, housing estates and closed transit sites.

item.title: What Are the Backrooms Levels? From Level 0 to The End — and Why There Is No Official Canon
item.description: A plain-language guide to the Backrooms levels, from Level 0 to The End, covering only the ones people actually talk about. Plus an answer to the real question: why do the wikis contradict each other?

item.title: What Are the Poolrooms? Where the Blue-Tiled Water Spaces Came From, and Where to Feel Them in Japan
item.description: Also known as Backrooms Level 37, the Poolrooms are among the most shared liminal images online. Here is where they actually came from, why they feel frightening and nostalgic at once, and where to find that atmosphere in Japan.

item.title: Where Was the Original Backrooms Photo Taken? The Real Building, Identified in 2024
item.description: One photograph posted to 4chan in 2019 created the Backrooms. Its location stayed unknown for five years, until internet researchers pinned it down in 2024. Here is where, when, and why that picture was taken.

item.title: Backrooms vs Exit 8: Two Endless Spaces That Work in Opposite Ways
item.description: Empty, uniform, no visible way out. The Backrooms and Exit 8 get compared constantly, but their fear is structured in opposite ways. Here is how each came about, and what actually separates them.

item.title: Who Is Kane Pixels? From a Post at Sixteen to Directing for A24
item.description: Kane Parsons, known online as Kane Pixels, defined what the Backrooms looks like and became an A24 feature director at twenty. His background, key works, the Blender-only workflow, and his stance on generative AI.

item.title: Noclip Meaning: What Noclip Is, and How a Game Term Came to Describe the Back of Reality
item.description: Every explanation of the Backrooms uses the word noclip. It started as a debug feature for walking through walls. Here is where the term came from, and why one word became the core of an internet legend.

item.title: Do You Need to Do Homework Before Watching Backrooms? The Legend, the YouTube Series, and the Director
item.description: Backrooms opened in Japan on September 4, 2026. Do you need to know anything going in? We answer that, then trace the 2019 4chan urban legend, the Kane Pixels YouTube series the film is based on, and director Kane Parsons, who debuted with A24 at twenty.

item.title: Is "Exit 8" Real? Looking for Actual Places With the Same Eerie Vibe
item.description: The horror game (and film) Exit 8 feels unsettlingly real. Instead of hunting for "the one station," we round up real places in Japan with that same liminal vibe, mapped on LIMap.
